title: The next chapter for CI/CD in Fabric Warehouse (Preview)
author: pradeepsvs

content.text:
Building and operating a data warehouse is increasingly a software engineering discipline. Teams want to develop warehouse changes in isolation, version them in Git, review them through pull requests, promote them safely across environments, and automate the entire process using their existing CI/CD systems.
Over the past several releases, we've been evolving CI/CD in Fabric Warehouse around that lifecycle:
• DacFx established a common schema deployment foundation.
• Pre, and post-deployment scripts expanded deployments beyond schema changes.
• Warehouse Item Definition APIs opened the same lifecycle to automation.
Together, these investments are creating a more complete CI/CD lifecycle for Fabric Warehouse, from developing and versioning database changes to deploying and automating them across environments. Let’s take a closer look at how each capability moves that experience forward, what’s available today, and what we’re building next.
What we've delivered
Establishing a consistent deployment foundation with DacFx
The first challenge was making Warehouse deployments behave like database deployments, not artifact copies. A Warehouse contains state, data, dependencies, and relationships between database objects. Moving a change from development to production therefore requires understanding what changed and how those changes should be applied to the target database.
This is where DacFx became foundational to the experience. With Git Integration, it is represented as a SQL database project in source control. Developers can work using familiar Git practices such as branching, commits, and pull requests. When those changes are synchronized back to Fabric, DacFx understands the database model and determines the schema changes that need to be applied.
Figure: Git-based development workflow in Microsoft Fabric, enabling isolated feature development, collaboration through pull requests, and synchronization of Fabric items across feature and shared workspaces, with infrastructure managed as code.
We extended that same foundation to deployment pipelines. When a Warehouse moves between development, test and production environments, DacFx compares source and target states and generates the incremental deployment required to move the target to the desired state.
Figure: End-to-end CI/CD workflow in Microsoft Fabric, combining Git-based feature development with deployment pipelines to promote Fabric items consistently across development, test, and production environments.
That established a consistent path: Develop → Version in Git → Review → Deploy → Validate → Promote.
Pre, and post-deployment scripts
A production deployment rarely consists of schema changes alone. Teams often need to prepare data before a deployment, seed or initialize data afterward, or execute SQL actions that need to happen at a specific point in the release. To support that workflow, we introduced pre, and post-deployment scripts.
A shared SQL query can be designated as a pre, or post-deployment script and becomes part of the SQL project. The designation travels with the Warehouse through Git, allowing those actions to be versioned and deployed together with the database definition. The resulting deployment lifecycle becomes pre-deployment actions → DacFx schema deployment → post-deployment actions
Figure: Pre, and post-deployment script configuration in Fabric Warehouse, enabling developers to define SQL scripts that execute automatically before and after schema deployment as part of the CI/CD lifecycle.
This moves more of the database release process into the CI/CD definition rather than leaving teams to coordinate separate manual steps. Learn more about pre and post-deployment scripts.
Warehouse Item Definition APIs
Git integration and deployment pipelines provide built-in Fabric experiences, but enterprise CI/CD also needs to work outside the Fabric portal. Customers have existing build systems, automation frameworks and release pipelines and need a programmatic way to manage Warehouse definitions.
Warehouse Item Definition APIs are the next part of that foundation. Warehouse definitions support SQL project and DACPAC formats, and Fabric APIs can be used to create a Warehouse from a definition, retrieve its current definition, or update it programmatically. Learn more about the Warehouse REST APIs. This means the same Warehouse definition that underpins Git integration can also participate in API-driven CI/CD workflows.
Bringing Familiar Warehouse Development Experiences to Client Tools
A complete CI/CD experience starts well before deployment. Developers need familiar tools to build, compare, validate, and manage database changes throughout the development lifecycle. Alongside our DacFx investments, we've strengthened Fabric Warehouse support across SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS) and Visual Studio Code, bringing familiar SQL development workflows closer to the Fabric web experience.
These investments include:
• Database project support in SSMS: Develop and manage Warehouse schemas using SQL database projects and familiar database development workflows.
• Schema Compare in VS Code: Compare database schemas, review differences, and generate the changes needed to synchronize environments.
• Consistent database development: Use the same SQL project and DacFx foundation whether developing in the Fabric portal or client tools.
• Pre, and post-deployment scripts: Maintain deployment scripts as part of the database project, enabling a consistent deployment experience across web-based and client-based development workflows.
The goal is simple: developers should be able to choose their preferred development environment without changing how their database projects are versioned, built, or deployed.
This brings together the flexibility of familiar SQL development tools with the integrated CI/CD experience in Fabric Warehouse.
What's next for CI/CD in Fabric Warehouse
Building on this foundation, we’re focusing on three investments:
• Deployment configurations: Give developers control over how changes are applied. Cover data handling, object handling, and error handling. Apply different behaviors per environment, such as permissive in development and stricter in production.
• Fabric CI/CD package (fabric-cicd) support for Warehouse: Simplify end-to-end automation. Deploy Warehouse definitions from source control alongside other Fabric items. Integrate with systems like Azure DevOps and GitHub Actions.
• CI/CD for SQL analytics endpoint: Extend Git integration and deployment pipelines using the same SQL project and DacFx foundation. Lay the groundwork for coordinated deployments across dependent Fabric items in medallion and data mesh architectures.
The goal: Move from CI/CD for individual items to a consistent, predictable, automated lifecycle for interconnected Fabric analytics solutions.
Get started with CI/CD in Fabric Warehouse
• Connect your Warehouse to Git: Set up Git integration to version your Warehouse as a SQL database project and develop changes in isolation.
• Promote changes across environments: Use deployment pipelines to move Warehouse changes from development to test and production.
• Automate data actions around your releases: Configure pre and post-deployment scripts so data preparation and seeding travel with your database definition.
• Integrate with your existing CI/CD systems: Use the Warehouse REST APIs to create, retrieve, and update Warehouse definitions programmatically.
Try these capabilities today and share your feedback in Fabric Ideas | Microsoft Fabric Community. Your input directly shapes what we build next for CI/CD in Fabric Warehouse.
